newsitem.title: USA: Ford pact heads for vote as GM, Chrysler bargain.
newsitem.headline: Ford pact heads for vote as GM, Chrysler bargain.

text.p: Ford Motor Co.'s U.S. hourly workers are expected to swiftly ratify a rich new United Auto Workers contract this weekend as the union continues talks with both General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp.
"The decision still hasn't been made as to where we're going to concentrate our bargaining next," UAW spokesman Bobbie Barbee said Friday.
UAW President Stephen Yokich met with top negotiators at both companies earlier this week to help move the talks forward, Barbee said.
Bargaining in subcommittees at both GM and Chrysler was expected to continue over the weekend, company and union officials said.
"All issues are being discussed," said a person familiar with GM's negotiations.

Industry observers had expected the UAW, which reached an agreement with Ford on September 17, to bargain next with Chrysler because the Canadian Auto Workers union is now threatening to strike GM's Canadian operations.
But Yokich has consistently delayed decisions on bargaining targets throughout the 1996 negotiations to gain leverage over the automakers.

Analysts say Chrysler can easily afford the provisions of the Ford contract, which require the company to maintain jobs for about 95 percent of its current 105,000-member hourly UAW workforce during the pact's three-year term. But the pact is expected to cause problems for GM, which needs to shrink its workforce to cut costs to competitive levels.

UAW officials expect Ford workers to approve the pact by an overwhelming margin. The deal provides $13,900 in economic gains for the average worker over the life of the pact, plus substantial increases in pension benefits, and $1,000 per child per year in college tuition assistance.
"It's viewed very favorably in our plant," Carl Dowell, president of Local 862 in Louisville, Ky., said of the agreement.
Final results of the voting are expected to be announced on Monday.

Meanwhile, the leader of the Canadian Auto Workers said Friday that he told the top executive of a prospective buyer of two of GM's Canadian parts plants that the union would insist that he honor terms of the next GM contract.
CAW President Buzz Hargrove declined to identify the buyer, but UAW officials have identified it as Joseph, Littlejohn & Levy, a New York-based investment firm.
"I told him, 'You can buy if you want. You buy us, but you also buy the CAW-GM master collective agreement,'" Hargrove told reporters.

Joseph, Littlejohn & Levy also is negotiating to buy two of GM's U.S. parts plants, said Whitey Hale, president of UAW Local 326 at one of the facilities in Flint, Mich. The other plants are located in Livonia, Mich., and Windsor and Oshawa, Ontario.
Hale said he wants the UAW to take a tougher stance against the sale of the facilities, which make door hinges, window mechanisms, door panels and other interior trim parts.
"I think if our UAW leadership were more militant, they could save those plants. They should take a lesson from Hargrove," he said.
